channel.title: Genomics Feed
channel.description: Aggregated research articles from Nature Genetics, Cell Genomics, Genome Biology, Genome Research, Nucleic Acids Research, and RNA.

item.title: Genome Biology: Community benchmarking of generative models for privacy-preserving synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation
Nucleic Acids Research: Histone H3.3 subvariant H3mm15 is required for normal spermatogenesis by regulating gene expression
item.description: Abstract Histone H3 variants play a fundamental role in chromatin regulation, contributing to gene expression. While the functional diversity of H3.3 subvariants remains largely unexplored, we identified H3mm15 as a testis-expressed H3.3 subvariant that regulates meiotic transcription. Using RNA sequencing and variant-specific reverse-transcription quantitative PCR, we demonstrate here that H3mm15 is expressed predominantly in the testis. Loss of H3mm15 leads to seminiferous tubule disorganization and altered expression of spermatogenesis-related genes. Chromatin profiling reveals that H3mm15 is relatively enriched at promoter-proximal regions compared with H3.3, despite its lower overall chromatin incorporation and lower nucleosomal stability. Functional assays show that H3mm15 has a more moderate impact on transcriptional responses to stimuli than H3.3. Although H3mm15 forms a less stable nucleosome, its reduced stability does not confer enhanced transcription by RNAPII in vitro . Our findings suggest the existence of an H3.3 sub-barcode mechanism, in which structurally distinct H3.3 subvariants differentially regulate chromatin states and contribute to gene regulation during spermatogenesis.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
item.description: SAIGE-QTL is a framework for eQTL mapping that directly models single-cell read counts using a Poisson mixed model, achieving improved statistical efficiency and power and enabling rare variant set-based testing in the single-cell eQTL setting.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch
item.description: RSparsePro performs robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch by coupling a probabilistic graphical model with a variational inference algorithm, identifying credible sets with higher power and coverage than existing methods.

item.title: Nature Genetics: An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing
item.description: T cells provide a unique setting for quantification of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. The authors introduce TCRi, an information-theoretic framework for this, and find mutual information to be a robust determinant of immunotherapeutic response.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Multiscale multimodal integration of spatial omics through a deep generative model with CORAL
item.description: Cross-scale spatial Omics Registration and Analysis via graph Learning is a deep generative model that integrates multiscale spatial multi-omics data using graph-attention aggregation mechanisms, enabling a comprehensive spatial analysis.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Leveraging human pangenome for improved somatic variant detection
item.description: Fu et al. show that the human pangenome improves somatic-variant calling accuracy over GRCh38 and CHM13 and can infer donor-specific assemblies that reduce germline contamination and reveal functionally relevant somatic variants missed by GRCh38 in cancer, thereby offering a scalable alternative to costly de novo assemblies.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Notch/NF-κB crosstalk signaling controls SASP gene expression during brain aging
item.description: Abstract Brain aging is associated with chronic, low-grade inflammation known as inflammaging, which is largely driven by senescent glial cells secreting pro-inflammatory factors termed as senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). In humans, the release of SASP factors in the brain is linked with an increased risk for the development of neurodegenerative disorders; thus, elucidating the underlying molecular mechanisms is essential for understanding the pathophysiology of brain aging. Both NF-κB and Notch signaling are known to regulate SASP expression; however, their mode of interaction in brain inflammaging is poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that brain aging is broadly associated with NF-κB activation but Notch suppression using different transgenic mouse models. Astrocytic NF-κB activation in young mice was able to mimic premature SASP formation but repressed Notch signaling in parallel. Bioinformatic analyses further identified conserved crosstalk sites within SASP genes co-occupied by Notch/RBPJ and NF-κB transcription factors in vivo , allowing specific combinatorial regulation. Importantly, selective physical interactions enable that activated Notch can act as a negative modulator of NF-κB signaling at different molecular levels. Consistently, pharmacological activation of Notch in primary astrocytes significantly reduced NF-κB-driven SASP gene expression. Together, these findings identify Notch–NF-κB crosstalk as a potential therapeutic target to mitigate brain inflammaging.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: New pathogenic ZNHIT3 variants causing fetal hydrops and lethality disrupt snoRNP assembly
item.description: Abstract ZNHIT3 is a conserved assembly factor required for biogenesis of box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) complexes, which are key players in ribosome biogenesis. Pathogenic variants in ZNHIT3 cause Progressive Encephalopathy with Edema, Hypsarrhythmia, and Optic Atrophy (PEHO) syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder typically recognized postnatally. Here, we describe two fetuses from a single family who developed isolated hydrops in the early second trimester of pregnancy, resulting in intrauterine demise. Whole-genome quartet sequencing identified two new ZNHIT3 variants, c.40T > C; p.(Cys14Arg) and c.251_254del; p.(Glu84Alafs*8), inherited from healthy parents that present as compound heterozygous alleles in both fetuses. Functional studies using a ZNHIT3 knockdown-rescue system in HEK293T cells demonstrated impaired proliferation and increased apoptosis and revealed distinct molecular consequences for the two variants. One variant produced a stable ZNHIT3 protein lacking the region required for interaction with NUFIP1 and efficient box C/D snoRNP assembly, whereas the second variant reduced ZNHIT3 protein abundance. Both variants impaired snoRNP assembly, reduced the abundance of select box C/D snoRNAs, and caused site-specific losses of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) 2′-O-methylation. These defects were accompanied by changes in ribosome biogenesis and reduced translational output. Together, our findings expand the phenotypic spectrum associated with ZNHIT3 deficiency to include severe antenatal disease and demonstrate that impaired box C/D snoRNP assembly and rRNA modification represent convergent molecular consequences of pathogenic ZNHIT3 variants.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Transcription factor CCTF1 plays an important role in regulating proteasome activity during archaeal cell division
item.description: Abstract Archaea of the order Sulfolobales exhibit a highly ordered cell cycle progression similar to that of eukaryotes. It has been demonstrated that degradation of the cell division protein CdvB by the proteasome controls the progression of cell division. However, how the proteasome itself is regulated during the cell cycle is not fully understood. Recently, the cyclically expressed ArsR (arsenical resistance operon repressor) family transcription factor CCTF1 (cell cycle transcription factor 1) was shown to repress expression of PAN (proteasome-activating nucleotidase) in Sulfolobus acidocaldarius . Here, using biochemical approaches, comparative transcriptomics, and proteomics, we provide further insights into the CCTF1 function and show that it regulates PAN expression in Saccharolobus islandicus by binding to an AT-rich palindromic sequence within the pan promoter. We also reassessed the role of the cyclically expressed protein kinase aCcrK in the regulation of proteasome activity and conclude that CCTF1, rather than aCcrK, is the primary factor controlling the proteasome activity. These findings advance our understanding of the proteasome-mediated cell cycle regulation in archaea.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors
item.description: This longitudinal single-cell study of estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer suggests that strong estrogen signaling, ER-linked enhancers and active T cell responses could predict sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors, whereas resistance involves androgen signaling though hormone-sensing enhancer activity.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Systematic engineering of synthetic minimal promoters for tunable transgene expression in mammalian cells
item.description: Abstract Fine-tuning transgene levels is crucial in fundamental and applied research. Native promoters are broadly utilized to regulate transgene expression. However, their large size and structural complexity hinder predictable tuning, constrain compatibility with viral vectors with limited capacity, and increase the risk of homologous recombination. Synthetic promoters are short de novo sequences, typically consisting of an enhancer region, which is positioned upstream of a minimal promoter that determines transcription initiation efficiency. Enhancer optimization typically yields coarse activation shifts, alters response curves, and requires case-by-case optimization. Synthetic minimal promoter architecture enables fine-tuning that is potentially compatible with any enhancer region. In this study, we systematically optimized minimal promoter sequences, core element composition, and regulatory motif sequences. Our findings support a modular model of minimal promoter function in which cis- regulatory elements from different minimal promoters can be mixed, altered, added, or deleted to yield predictable expression outcomes. We shortened and thereby enhanced the efficiency of known minimal promoters, engineered modular tunable minimal promoters, and generated candidate regulatory elements spanning 7–8 nucleotides that drive efficient transcription when combined with artificial ${5^{\prime}}$ untranslated regions (5'UTRs) that function as an additional regulatory layer. This framework broadens the utility of synthetic promoters for next-generation applications.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: DNA mimic helical foldamers with up to 100 units: synthesis and recognition of a multiprotein complex
item.description: Abstract DNA mimic foldamers (DMFOs) are helically folded aromatic oligoamides that mimic the shape and charge distribution of double-stranded B-DNA. DMFOs consist of an alternation of two amino acid monomers, M and Q. Here, we introduce a new synthetic approach of (MQ) n oligomers on solid phase that enabled the production of sequences as long as a 100mer, formally equivalent to a 50-base pair DNA duplex. The approach takes advantage of dimeric Fmoc-MQ-OH as building blocks. Three such macromonomers were synthesized using Q and M units bearing different side chains. Solid phase synthesis protocols were validated in all series. Helix handedness was shown to be determined by a single chiral residue. The purified long oligomers were analyzed by reversed phase HPLC, mass spectrometry, circular dichroism, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy for their purity, identity, and helix-handedness bias. Clusters of foldamers forming in the presence of Ca 2+ could be visualized by cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Lastly, a 72mer DMFO was shown to bind to the A-module of the chromatin remodeling complex INO80 slightly tighter than a comparable DNA duplex. A cryo-EM structure of the complex at a resolution of 3.59 Å showed that the DMFO occupies the A-module DNA binding region.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Detection and quantification of DNA double-strand breaks by genomic and imaging methods: a critical appraisal of capabilities and limitations
item.description: Abstract DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are the most genotoxic form of DNA damage. Unrepaired DSBs may cause loss of chromosome fragments at mitosis, while incorrectly repaired DSBs can cause chromosome aberrations and other adverse effects, leading to cell cycle arrest, senescence, cell death, or neoplastic transformation. Detecting and quantifying DSBs is important in studies of genome instability, aging, and cancer. Methods of detecting and quantifying DSBs fall into two broad categories: imaging-based methods, used to detect and localize DNA breaks in individual cells, and genomic methods, a new category utilizing massively parallel DNA sequencing to map DSBs genome-wide in a cell population. Imaging and genomic methods yield fundamentally different information. This review focuses on a critical evaluation of the capabilities and limitations of genomic and imaging methods for the detection and quantification of DSBs. It explains why the class of genomic methods, where quantification is based on counting the detected unique DSBs and the number of cells in the sample, results in inaccurate assessment of the average number of DSBs per cell and how this problem can be solved. We also discuss complementarity of genomic and imaging methods and potential directions of their future development.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Coupling metabolic enhancement to plasmid spread enables programmable antimicrobial control
item.description: Abstract The rise of multidrug-resistant pathogens underscores the need for precise antimicrobial strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Conjugation-based approaches offer a powerful yet underexploited means of delivering targeted genetic interventions within microbial communities. Here, we combine selective killing modules with optimized conjugative vectors to target antibiotic-resistant pathogens and clinically relevant resistance plasmids. First, we engineered toxin–intein modules, programmable cassettes that restrict toxic activity to specific regulatory contexts. We developed modules targeting Shigella spp., Salmonella enterica , and bacteria carrying the resistance plasmid pOXA-48, demonstrating tunable and selective activity at both species and strain levels. To identify the optimal delivery platform, we compared mobilizable and conjugative plasmids, finding that conjugative systems consistently outperform mobilizable ones by approximately one order of magnitude. We then streamlined the broad-host-range plasmid RP4 and enhanced its functionality by incorporating the metabolic fos locus, a type IV pilus operon or both features combined. Integration of the anti-pOXA-48 module into these vectors enabled effective suppression of resistance plasmid spread in complex microbial communities. Together, these results advance the use of conjugative plasmids as programmable antimicrobial platforms and identify delivery efficiency and ecological competitiveness as key determinants of the success of such interventions.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: CFDP1 is required for histone variant H2A.Z deposition by the human SRCAP chromatin remodeling complex
item.description: Abstract Craniofacial Developmental Protein 1 (CFDP1) is a member of the evolutionarily conserved family of Bucentaur (BCNT) proteins and is required for cell survival and differentiation during tooth development. Its yeast homolog is involved in histone variant H2A.Z deposition by the yeast SWR1C remodeler. Direct connections between CFDP1, H2A.Z deposition, and the mammalian SWR1 homolog, Snf2-Related CREBBP Activator Protein (SRCAP), are poorly understood. Here, we perform detailed biochemical reconstitution and characterization of the human SRCAP complex (SRCAP-C). We find that CFDP1 weakly interacts with SRCAP-C in a salt concentration-dependent manner and is essential for H2A.Z dimer exchange by SRCAP-C. We show that CFDP1 stimulates the basal ATPase activity of reconstituted SRCAP-C, suggesting a requirement for CFDP1 in regulating intrinsic catalytic ATPase activity. Additionally, CFDP1 deficiency in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) leads to a genome-wide reduction of H2A.Z, H3K27me3, and H3K4me3 deposition, accompanied by the upregulation of developmental genes normally marked by these modifications. Taken together, our results provide mechanistic insights into how CFDP1 regulates histone variant H2A.Z deposition by SRCAP-C. Given mutations in the SRCAP gene cause Floating-Harbor syndrome, a rare, dominant developmental disorder, our study provides an additional link between craniofacial development and SRCAP-mediated H2A.Z deposition.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A framework for genome-wide characterization of DNA methylation and variant effect prediction
item.description: This study introduces a framework for integrating DNA methylation data across more than 90 tissues and cell types, characterizing genome-wide methylation patterns and predicting context-specific effects of genetic variants on DNA methylation and regulatory function using a deep learning model, Wreath.

item.title: Nature Genetics: AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors
item.description: Stefan et al. present MANTIS, an AI model to predict individualized survival in childhood brain tumors from routine DNA methylation profiling. MANTIS may help identify patients who benefit from less intense treatment to reduce lifelong side effects.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Multi-platform framework for mapping somatic retrotransposition in human tissues
item.description: Wang et al. establish a systematically benchmarked framework integrating long reads and genome assemblies for accurate detection and source tracing of somatic mobile element insertions. Applied to normal human tissues, this framework reveals rare somatic L1 insertions, enabling studies of how mobile elements reshape genomes during life.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: The African swine fever virus I73R protein is a multifunctional Zα domain that mediates both Z-binding-dependent and -independent biological functions through induction of phase separation
item.description: Abstract African swine fever virus (ASFV) I73R encodes a protein consisting only of a Zalpha (Zα) domain. Here, we studied its biochemical properties. Complementary approaches demonstrated that I73R is a multifunctional Zα domain that combines Z-binding, B-to-Z conversion, and liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) induction activities. I73R proved to be a better converter than human ADAR1 Zα, and it retained conversion activity with Y48I mutation of its Z-binding site. Next, we investigated I73R biological functions, leading to the following findings: (i) Ectopic expression of I73R or mutated I73R with deficient Z-binding both inhibited arsenite-induced stress granules to a similar extent, and none of these proteins localized within these organelles. (ii) I73R formed cytosolic condensates with dsRNA, Z-DNA, and Z-RNA in ASFV-infected cells. (iii) Rescuing of ASFV I73R deletion by sequences encoding natural, mutated, and chimeric forms of Zα domains demonstrated that I73R mediated both Z-binding-dependent and -independent biological functions through induction of LLPS. This conclusion was further supported by the effect of the LLPS inhibitor 1,6-hexanediol on the replication of ASFV I73R recombinant strains. This study further demonstrates the functional diversity that exists among Zα domains. It unravels new outlooks targeting Zα domain-mediated LLPS for the development of pharmaceutical molecules able to regulate viral and cellular Zα domain-containing proteins.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Varied Ensembles of Long-range ChROmatin interactions drive chromatin compartmentalization
item.description: Abstract The chromatin components that are involved in organizing eukaryotic genomes into active and inactive compartments remain unclear. In analysing viable Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking different chromatin-regulatory proteins, we found that the HP1-type factor HPL-2 and the MBT-domain protein LIN-61 jointly contribute to chromatin compartmentalization. Genomic regions bound by both proteins and their cognate histone mark H3 lysine 9 dimethylation (H3K9me2) form broad interfaces of 30–50 kilobases that engage in combinatorial interactions, which we term ‘Varied Ensembles of Long-range ChROmatin interactions’ (VELCROs). Remarkably, VELCROs are defined by high density of H3K9me2, HPL-2, and LIN-61 sites, but not by the intensity of their individual peaks. Mutants that display defective chromatin compartmentalization are impaired in VELCROs. Polymer simulations show that VELCROs can drive a phase transition that segregates B from A chromatin compartments depending on peak densities. Our work identifies VELCROs as stochastic ensembles of interactions constrained within defined chromatin hubs that shape genome compartmentalization.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Monomeric ZRANB3 drives replication fork reversal
item.description: Abstract Replication fork reversal is a central response to replication stress, yet how a SNF2 translocase coordinates the distinct mechanical steps required for this reaction remains elusive. Here, we define the mechanism by which ZRANB3 catalyzes fork reversal using biochemical, biophysical, and single-molecule approaches. ZRANB3 binds fork DNA as a monomer at the junction, establishing the minimal functional unit required for activity. Mechanistically, ZRANB3 combines ATP-dependent localized duplex opening with ATP-independent strand annealing to facilitate four-way junction formation, followed by directional branch migration that supports long-range fork reversal. Single-molecule fluorescence analyses further demonstrate that monomeric ZRANB3 is sufficient to drive fork reversal. Together, these findings define how ZRANB3 integrates distinct DNA remodeling activities within a single enzyme to catalyze fork reversal.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Clonal hematopoiesis and cytopenias following CAR19 therapy
item.description: This study shows that clonal hematopoiesis expands after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy and contributes to secondary myeloid cancers. In addition, the CAR vector frequently integrates into pre-existing clonal hematopoiesis.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A catalog of transcriptome genetic regulation in a consanguineous Middle Eastern biobank
item.description: This study reports an atlas of transcriptomic genetic effects from a Middle Eastern population biobank, revealing population-specific regulatory variants and links to clinically relevant traits.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Physical determinants of reliable RNA–ligand binding prediction revealed by P-RISE
item.description: Abstract RNA-targeted small-molecule discovery is challenged by the scarcity of experimentally characterized RNA–ligand complexes and by the limited transferability of current computational approaches across chemically diverse systems. Here we present P-RISE, a physics-grounded framework for RNA–ligand binding prediction, and use it to identify the physical determinants underlying reliable performance. Systematic evaluation of force fields, ionic environments, dielectric treatments, and entropy corrections reveals three coupled requirements: preservation of RNA-binding pocket integrity under ion-sensitive conditions; an effective electrostatic error cancellation regime enabled by an elevated internal dielectric constant; and an empirically observed coupling between entropy correction and solvent modeling. Integrating these features, P-RISE provides stable affinity ranking, physics-grounded delineation of its physicochemical applicability domain, accurate metal ion site localization, and improved binding pose discrimination relative to established RNA docking and scoring approaches. Crucially, benchmarking against AlphaFold3 reveals that co-folding models, optimized for structure generation rather than energetic ranking, benefit from an explicit physics-based evaluation layer. Furthermore, diverse machine-learning comparisons demonstrate that purely data-driven methods lack stability and generalization in this data-poor regime. Ultimately, P-RISE provides a mechanistic understanding of RNA–ligand modeling, serving as a principled physical baseline that defines reliable prediction boundaries, and guides future data-driven integration.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: RNA viruses can exploit self-cleaving ribozymes for translation initiation
item.description: Abstract Small self-cleaving ribozymes are catalytic RNAs discovered in viroid-like agents, which are replicating circular RNAs (circRNAs) postulated as relics of a prebiotic RNA world. In the last decade, however, small ribozymes have also been detected across the tree of life, from bacterial to human genomes, and more recently, in unusual circRNA viruses. Here we report the conserved occurrence of diverse small ribozymes within the linear genomes of typical single- and double-stranded RNA viruses infecting fungi and plants. We identified type I hammerhead ribozymes in the 5′-UTRs of chrysovirids and fusarivirids, displaying self-cleaving activity in vitro and in vivo . Similar hammerhead, as well as hepatitis delta and twister ribozymes, occur in diverse megabirna-, hypo-, fusagra-, toti-, or tombus-like viruses. The ribozymes appear as isolated motifs within the UTRs or as tandem pairs that encompass small RNA segments (186–399 nt) resembling Zetavirus-like sequences. In vivo characterization of the 5′-UTR from a fungal chrysovirus revealed that its RNA self-cleaving activity is essential for protein translation initiation. Analogous experiments in plants with diverse ribozyme motifs confirmed that self-cleaving activity alone can induce cap-independent translation. We conclude that RNA self-cleaving activity, historically linked to the rolling circle replication of viroid-like circRNAs, appears to be co-opted by some linear RNA viruses for translational roles.

item.title: Genome Biology: Comprehensive evaluation of antibody language models across multiple antibody design tasks
Nucleic Acids Research: Region-specific generation and retention of acetylated cohesin shape the genome-wide pattern of sister chromatid cohesion
item.description: Abstract Sister chromatid cohesion depends on ESCO2-mediated acetylation of the cohesin subunit SMC3, yet how this modification is established and maintained across the genome remains poorly understood. Here, we examined the chromatin-binding dynamics of ESCO2 and its enzymatic activity using quantitative ChIP-seq of human cells synchronously progressing through S phase. ESCO2 bound broadly along chromosomes without forming discrete peaks and preferentially localized to transcriptionally inactive regions, but was not confined to H3K9me3- or H3K27me3-enriched heterochromatin. Consistent with this binding pattern, ESCO2-dependent SMC3 acetylation showed a similarly broad distribution in these regions. In contrast, ESCO1, a paralog of ESCO2, primarily mediated SMC3 acetylation at cohesin peak sites. Notably, most of the broadly distributed, ESCO2-dependent SMC3 acetylation generated during S phase was progressively lost from chromatin after replication, whereas the fraction that persisted into late G2 accumulated in domains enriched for the repressive H3K27me3 modification. Our work identifies selective post-replicative retention of acetylated cohesin as a previously unappreciated step in shaping the genome-wide architecture of sister chromatid cohesion.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Integrator complex removes lesion-stalled RNA polymerase II after transcription-coupled repair to facilitate transcription restart
item.description: Abstract Gene transcription by RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) is highly vulnerable to transcription-blocking DNA lesions (TBLs), which, if unresolved, induce transcription stress leading to cellular decline and aging. TBLs are removed by transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER). TC-NER is initiated when Cockayne syndrome group B protein recognizes lesion-stalled Pol II and promotes TC-NER complex assembly. This complex recruits TFIIH for lesion verification, followed by incision and repair to enable transcription restart. Many TBLs stall Pol II within its active site, shielding the lesion from repair and requiring Pol II processing to expose it. However, whether this occurs through Pol II backtracking or release from the DNA, and the regulatory mechanisms involved, remain poorly defined. Here, we identified the Integrator complex as a key factor in lesion-stalled Pol II processing. Interaction proteomics revealed Integrator recruitment to late-stage TC-NER complexes. Integrator’s endonuclease core promotes efficient transcription recovery after TBL induction, without affecting lesion removal by TC-NER. Live-cell imaging and chromatin retention assays demonstrated that Integrator facilitates Pol II release from DNA following TC-NER. Collectively, these findings support a two-step mechanism for Pol II clearance during TC-NER, wherein TFIIH-mediated backtracking exposes the lesion for repair, followed by Integrator-mediated Pol II release to restore transcription.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Queuosine-modification dependent histidyl tRNA fragment promotes cell-type dependent proliferation
item.description: Abstract tRNA fragments (tRFs) are natural, small non-coding RNAs produced by endogenous ribonucleolytic cleavage of tRNAs. tRFs play a role in many biological pathways, including regulation of cell proliferation. Specific tRNA modifications affect tRF biogenesis. Queuosine (Q) modification occurs at the wobble anticodon nucleotide of 4 mammalian tRNAs and protects these tRNAs from fragmentation. Here, we investigated cell-type and tRNA Q-modification dependencies on mammalian cell proliferation. We found that Q-modified tRNA can either increase, decrease, or make no difference in proliferation. Proliferation decreased in MCF7, a breast cancer cell line, when tRNAs were Q-modified and dependent on the modification enzyme complex, QTRT1/2. MCF7 proliferation increases upon the transfection of Q-modification-dependent tRF His or decreases upon knockdown of endogenous tRF His . Consistent with Q-dependent proliferation reduction, polysome profiling showed decreased translation efficiency of ribosomal proteins. Finally, protein pull-down of MCF7 lysates using tRF His identified Musashi RNA-binding protein 2 (Msi2) as a tRF His -binding protein. Msi2 knockdown reduced the Q-modification-dependent or tRF His dependent cell proliferation effect. Our results illustrate a highly cell-type-dependent proliferation effect of tRNA Q-modification, suggesting multi-faceted mechanisms in studying this ubiquitous tRNA modification.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Data analysis of experimentally solved nucleosome arrays reveals heterogeneous features
item.description: Abstract Atomic-resolution nucleosome array structures have provided invaluable information on eukaryotic genome packing. Although these arrays are often obtained for regular fibers with designed sequences, such information complements in vivo genome organization data and modeling studies. Here, we analyze such systems with a focus on chromatin organization. We highlight both robust and unique features, as well as suitable average values for coarse-grained modeling, such as the relative orientation and positioning of neighboring nucleosomes, and opening of the linker DNA. Our associated web resource (https://www.biomath.nyu.edu/chromstruct/) shares these collected systems and provides tools for their analysis. The heterogeneous features exhibit a wide range of geometrical properties that depend on linker DNA length, core histone protein variants, auxiliary protein binding, and fiber interdigitation. Yet experimental fiber geometries can be reproduced reasonably using average parameters, as demonstrated here by simulations with our mesoscale model for regular fibers and as reported separately for life-like systems with epigenetic marks. Such analysis may also be useful for modular design of chromatin fibers. The structural characterization of these chromatin building blocks provides new insights into the regulation of chromatin architecture and has implications for the modular design of chromatin fibers.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Structural probing of RNA hairpins quantifies protein occupancy on RNA and links it to function in human cells
item.description: Abstract RNA structures that form inside living cells govern processes ranging from translation to RNA decay, many of which are controlled by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). Because RBP specificity can depend on both RNA sequence and folding, traditional pulldown-based methods often obscure the structural context of bound RNAs. Here, a quantitative framework based on dimethyl sulfate mutational profiling and sequencing was established to directly measure RNA structure and RBP binding in human cells at single-nucleotide resolution. Applied to a 1600-member MS2 hairpin library, this approach revealed that RNA folding is the strongest determinant of MS2 coat protein (MCP) recognition in the MS2–MCP system, requiring formation of a stable hairpin and a consensus loop sequence, with stem length or GC content contributing primarily through their effect on hairpin folding. An in-cell occupancy model was derived to quantify fractional binding from structural readouts. Complementary systems using degron-tuned MCP and a downregulatory MCP fusion demonstrated binding behavior under subsaturating protein concentrations and showed that inferred occupancy quantitatively predicts RNA degradation efficiency. Together, these results establish a quantitative strategy for measuring RBP–RNA specificity and affinity directly in cells, using the MS2–MCP system to link RNA structure, protein occupancy, and regulatory outcome.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: The HELLS–MCM5 axis coordinates transcription–replication dynamics to preserve genomic integrity in ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma
item.description: Abstract The chromatin remodeler HELLS acts as a pleiotropic guardian of genomic integrity, orchestrating critical processes from DNA replication to DNA damage repair. In anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), HELLS functions as a transcriptional sentinel, fine-tuning chromatin accessibility and RNA polymerase II kinetics to sustain the oncogenic transcriptional landscape essential for lymphomagenesis. Here we show that HELLS preserves genomic stability and sustains ALK-negative ALCL proliferation by preventing transcription–replication conflicts. HELLS acts as a global regulator of R-loop homeostasis while transcriptionally sustaining MCM5, a core subunit of the replicative MCM2–7 complex, which locally restrains replication-transcription collisions at actively transcribed loci. Mechanistically, HELLS loss reduces MCM5 levels, triggering aberrant firing of origins within transcriptionally active regions and consequent collisions between replication forks and the transcription machinery. Being positioned distally from R-loop-enriched sites, HELLS and MCM5 cooperate to preserve genome integrity, with MCM5 acting as the effector that delivers locus-specific protection against replication-associated genomic instability. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of this axis increases R-loop burden and drastically reduces the survival of ALK-negative ALCL cells, providing a rationale for combination therapy. Collectively, the HELLS–MCM5 module emerges as a master coordinator of transcription–replication dynamics and a novel therapeutic vulnerability in aggressive lymphomas.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Dynamic phosphorylation of TCOF1 controlled by CK2 and PPM1D regulates nucleolar condensation and RNA polymerase I activity
item.description: Abstract The nucleolus is a membrane-less organelle essential for ribosomal DNA (rDNA) transcription and ribosome biogenesis, yet the mechanisms regulating its dynamic assembly remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the phosphatase protein phosphatase magnesium-dependent 1 delta (PPM1D) as a key regulator of the nucleolar architecture via dephosphorylation of the scaffold protein TCOF1. By combining super-resolution microscopy and domain mapping, we show that PPM1D localizes to the nucleolus through a conserved motif at the C-terminus. Phosphoproteomic analysis and structural modeling revealed that PPM1D targets casein kinase 2 (CK2)-phosphorylated sites within the low-complexity repeat domain of TCOF1, which impacts its interaction with RNA polymerase I (Pol I), immobilization in the fibrillar centres, and nucleolar condensation. Disruption of the phosphorylation balance by loss of PPM1D or inhibition of CK2 leads to nucleolar disorganization and reduced rDNA transcription. Finally, we demonstrate that pharmacological inhibition of PPM1D sensitizes cells to RNA Pol I inhibitors, in both p53-dependent and -independent contexts. Together, we uncover a reversible phosphorylation switch that governs TCOF1 dynamics and its nucleolar function, with potential implications for targeting ribosome biogenesis in cancer.

item.title: Genome Biology: Telomere-to-telomere genome of a dodecaploid desert shrub Prunus pedunculata reveals polyploidy-driven arid adaptation
Nucleic Acids Research: Metal-ion coordination drives active-site remodeling for backsplicing in circularly permuted group II introns
item.description: Abstract Circularly permuted (CP) group II introns are self-splicing ribozymes that undergo a sequential branching and backsplicing reaction to yield branched introns and circular exons (circRNAs). While the initial branching step is structurally characterized, the mechanistic principles that govern the subsequent large-scale active-site remodeling and stringent metal-ion specificity required for backsplicing remain poorly understood. Here, we present a series of high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the CP group II intron from Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus PAL5 ( Gdi -1), capturing the ribozyme at discrete stages along the branching -to- backsplicing pathway under distinct ionic conditions. Comparative analyses under K + /Mg 2+ , K + /Ca 2+ , and Cs + /Mg 2+ conditions demonstrate that productive backsplicing relies on ion-specific coordination networks that govern 3′ splice site (3′SS) docking and catalytic center formation, revealing the precise metal-ion-coordinated conformational rearrangements and dynamic splice-site exchange mechanisms. Crucially, we identify a previously unrecognized, highly selective monovalent cation-binding site, K3, that structurally couples the γ–γ′ interaction to reassembly of the heteronuclear four-metal core, thereby promoting productive second-step active-site formation. Together, these findings establish a structural basis for metal-ion-dependent active-site remodeling during group II intron catalysis and provide mechanistic insights into metal-ion selectivity in circRNA biogenesis.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Biobank-scale self-supervised genotype pretraining yields transferable representations for human genetics
item.description: Abstract Biobank-scale genotyping has created unprecedented cohorts for human genetics, yet the field still lacks scalable methods for learning transferable representations from largely unlabeled individual-level genotype data. Here, we introduce SNPBERT, a self-supervised transformer pretrained on genotypes from 485 923 UK Biobank participants using masked rsID prediction. SNPBERT embeddings recovered known population structure across UK Biobank and three external datasets, performed comparably to principal component analysis, and supported the identification of ancestry-informative marker SNPs. Fine-tuning with an attention-based multiple-instance head generated disease-specific risk scores that provided complementary information beyond conventional polygenic risk scores. The relative increase in Nagelkerke’s R 2 ranged from 0.7% to 3.3%, and independent associations were observed for seven of the eight chronic diseases examined. In celiac disease, attention prioritization recapitulated major histocompatibility complex signals while elevating variants in CCHCR1 and NOTCH4 relative to genome-wide association study (GWAS) ranking. These results support biobank-scale genotype pretraining as an early step toward foundation modeling for individual-level genotype data.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: The Mycobacterium tuberculosis Ku C-terminus orchestrates LigD activity through domain-specific interactions
item.description: Abstract Bacterial non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is a key DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair pathway that relies on the Ku–LigD complex to alleviate genomic instability. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis Ku C-terminus has been highlighted for its role in LigD recruitment to DSBs and stimulation of LigD ligase activity. However, it remains unclear how the Ku C-terminus interacts with and potentially influences other LigD activities. Here, we combine NMR spectroscopy, structural modelling, and mutational analysis to define the interaction interface between the Ku C-terminus and LigD. We identify critical residues in Ku (E246, V248, S258, K260, and N266) and the LigD polymerase (D162, V194, R198) and ligase (D522, K579, L580) domains that mediate this interaction. Functional assays reveal that Ku stimulates LigD ligase activity through contacts with both polymerase and ligase domains, while Ku attenuates template-dependent polymerase activity, contrasting previous studies in Pseudomonas aeruginosa homologs. Disrupting the Ku–LigD interface, either through Ku or LigD mutations, abolishes ligase stimulation and restores polymerase activity, highlighting a dual regulatory mechanism. Our data supports a model where Ku’s C-terminal region forms a bipartite interface with LigD to balance repair activity. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the Ku–LigD repair mechanism and uncovers species-specific differences in bacterial NHEJ.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: mobileRNA: an integrative, automated tool for accurate identification of mobile RNA molecules based on multiple genome mapping
item.description: Abstract RNA molecules can act as intercellular signals, with evidence of transport for both messenger RNA (mRNA) and small RNA over long distances. Such molecules that move from the cell in which they originated are termed mobile RNA. In grafted plants, when different genotypes are joined together, the movement of RNAs between tissues can be revealed by approaches that exploit natural polymorphisms between the genomes involved. However, current methods suffer from a high level of technological noise, and the lack of standardized approaches makes it challenging for researchers to robustly identify mobile RNA molecules. Here, we introduce an automated pipeline, mobileRNA , which uses a multi-genome approach based on simultaneous alignment of RNA sequencing data to merged reference genomes. We validated our approach using simulated grafting combinations and compared to other methods. When applying mobileRNA to real data, we find poor overlap to existing mobile mRNA annotations, consistent with recent studies that question the reliability of previously reported mobile mRNAs. Introducing a genome mappability index as a criterion for the likely success of detecting mobile RNAs, we find that SNP-based or two-step mapping approaches are inherently limited due to errors and poor mappability compared to cross-species grafting with large evolutionary distances.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: The 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein links the cell responses to transcription and replication stress by promoting replication fork reversal and homologous recombination
item.description: Abstract The 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (7SK-snRNP) releases positive transcription elongation factor b to sustain RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) activity during transcription stress. Many conditions that block transcription also cause replication stress, and 7SK-snRNP components have potential roles in transcription–replication conflicts and double-strand break (DSB) repair. Here, we investigate roles of 7SK-snRNP components in replication stress responses. We report that 7SK-snRNP promotes replication fork slowing in response to agents that cause both replication and transcription stress. Our data suggest that 7SK-snRNP facilitates RAD51-mediated replication fork reversal rather than transcription–replication conflicts. 7SK-snRNP also promotes RAD51 recruitment to replication-associated DSBs or post-replicative gaps under conditions of transcription stress and supports homologous recombination at direct DSBs. In contrast, 7SK-snRNP components are not required for RAD51 recruitment in response to hydroxyurea. Our data support that LARP7 functions during replication stress independently of its interaction with BRCA1, and that LARP7 and HEXIM1 promote survival of replication stress. 7SK-snRNP components are not recruited to stressed replication forks, and RNAPII inhibition phenocopies loss of these proteins. Our data support a model where 7SK-snRNP modulation of RNAPII activity helps facilitate several RAD51 functions under transcription stress conditions, thereby connecting the cell responses to transcription and replication stress.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: EWSR1 associates with the 40S ribosomal subunit and represses translation to maintain endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis
item.description: Abstract FET family proteins (FUS, EWSR1, and TAF15) have garnered significant attention due to their involvement in oncogenic fusions and mutations in various cancers and neurodegenerative disorders. Although these highly conserved RNA-binding proteins are widely described as multifunctional regulators of gene expression, their precise molecular functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized role for EWSR1 as a selective translational repressor in cancer cells. EWSR1 specifically targets mRNAs involved in lipid metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis. Loss of EWSR1 disrupts ER morphology and impairs activation of the unfolded protein response of the ER (UPR ER ). Mechanistically, EWSR1 represses translation upon association with target mRNAs, and its conserved region spanning two arginine–glycine–glycine (RGG) boxes contributes to association with the 40S ribosomal subunit. These findings define a novel role for EWSR1 in post-transcriptional gene regulation and suggest that perturbations in its translational activity may underlie the pathogenesis of FET-associated diseases.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Exploring DNA movement through the application of droplet-based high-efficiency chromatin conformation capture (DropHiChew) and loop velocity
item.description: Abstract This study presents a novel approach to understanding DNA movement dynamics. Chromatin conformation plays a crucial role in controlling gene expression and cellular processes, with abnormalities linked to diseases like cancer and genetic disorders. ​Current single-cell chromatin conformation methods face limitations in cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and capturing dynamic genome architecture.​​ Therefore, we develop ​DropHiChew, a droplet-based, highly efficient chromatin conformation capture method employing 10× Genomics single-cell systems for user-friendly, cost-effective implementation. Combined with our ​loop velocity algorithm—which estimates the speed and direction of cell development by quantifying chromatin movement—this approach accurately gauges the trajectory of DNA motion and cellular states even at shallow sequencing depth (50k contacts per cell). Validation demonstrates its applicability across biological systems, including HEK293T, spermiogenesis, and embryonic development. The integration of DropHiChew and loop velocity offers potential for diverse applications in chromatin capture studies. This paradigm provides a dynamic perspective on genome organization for disease modeling, cellular differentiation, and developmental biology.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: DNA defense systems become a fitness liability during plasmid conjugation
item.description: Abstract Horizontal gene transfer via conjugative plasmids is a major driver of bacterial evolution. While antibiotic exposure selects for the resistance genes carried by some plasmids, much uncertainty remains about how plasmids persist and spread in microbial communities in the absence of such external selection. Here, we show that conjugative plasmid transfer selectively reduces the fitness of non-permissive recipients through the process of lethal zygosis: a phenomenon in which repeated Type IV Secretion System (T4SS) engagement damages recipients that fail to establish the plasmid. We found that this contact-dependent antagonism effectively clears a niche for plasmid donors by turning recipients’ DNA defenses into a liability. Blocking establishment of the plasmid RK2 with CRISPR–Cas or restriction-modification caused strong fitness defects in Escherichia coli recipients by preventing expression of plasmid-encoded exclusion genes and leaving cells exposed to repeated T4SS engagement. We leveraged this insight to resolve an obstacle in bacterial editing by developing transposon vectors that co-deliver exclusion genes, increasing the efficiency of gene editing by orders of magnitude. Our results reveal the role of “coercive assimilation” in horizontal gene transfer, exposing a tradeoff where the advantage of bacterial immunity to foreign DNA is counterbalanced by increased susceptibility to lethal zygosis.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Population-scale single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of skeletal muscle reveals extensive context-specific genetic regulation
item.description: Single-nucleus chromatin accessibility and transcriptome maps of human skeletal muscle identify cell-state and context-specific QTLs that colocalize with genome-wide association signals for cardiometabolic traits.

item.description: Adeluwa et al. developed TFXcan, a framework that predicts personalized transcription factor binding from genotype data across ∼700 transcription-factor-tissue pairs. Applied to PrCa risk, TFXcan identified specific transcription factors and coordinated programs of transcription factors that drive the disease at risk loci.

item.title: Genome Biology: The glutamine-aspartate metabolic tradeoff between fast growth and metabolic flexibility
Nucleic Acids Research: Microsatellite expansion redirects chromatin modifiers to confer insect resistance to Bt bioinsecticides
item.description: Abstract Microsatellites are highly mutable genomic elements, yet their role in adaptive gene regulation in insects remains poorly understood. Here, we show that a tetranucleotide (ATGT) microsatellite expansion in the promoter of ABCC2 , a key Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin receptor gene, epigenetically silences its expression and confers resistance to Bt Cry1Ac toxin in Plutella xylostella (L.). Mechanistically, long repeats (≥27 units) in Cry1Ac-resistant strains preferentially recruit the histone methyltransferase E(z), promoting H3K27me2/3 deposition, chromatin compaction, and transcriptional silencing, whereas short repeats in susceptible strains maintain open chromatin through Tip60-mediated H4K5 acetylation. This repeat expansion alone is sufficient to repress ABCC2 , thereby conferring Bt resistance, while repeat length, chromatin state, and associated phenotypes partially revert under relaxed selection. These findings define a previously uncharacterized cis -acting element dynamically orchestrating insecticide resistance-associated gene expression and identify microsatellite-driven chromatin remodeling as a general and plastic regulatory strategy underlying rapid xenobiotic-resistance evolution in insects.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Uracil overload triggers global genome instability and dUTPdysgenesis
item.description: Abstract Uracil accumulation in DNA is a pervasive threat to genomic integrity, yet the global dynamics of how uracil overload drives genome instability remain elusive. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains with attenuated dUTPase ( DUT1 ) expression, we mapped the landscapes of genomic alterations including point mutations, recombination, and aneuploidy. Deletion of the UNG1 suppressed most induced mutations and loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH), identifying base excision repair as the primary driver of genomic alterations, whereas aneuploidy directly depends on the persistence of intact genomic uracil. Mechanistically, beyond localized bypass of static AP sites by translesion synthesis polymerases, the massive influx of uracil lesions induces a repair bottleneck by depleting Ung1 and Apn1. This resource titration, coupled with downstream processing intermediates, primarily drives mutagenesis at heterologous nonthymine positions. Furthermore, persistent static AP sites preferentially stimulate homologous recombination sub-pathway that yield interstitial LOH, whereas Apn1-mediated processing channels recombination toward terminal LOH. Crucially, we define a novel post-zygotic isolation mechanism, dUTPdysgenesis, where parental wild-type Ung1 unleashes an immediate enzymatic shock against a uracil-preloaded genome upon mating, triggering G1-phase chromosomal shattering and mutations. Collectively, this study transitions the paradigm of uracil mutagenesis from localized errors to a global engine of genome instability, bridging nucleotide metabolism, DNA repair kinetics, and speciation barriers.

item.title: Genome Biology: Urbanisation drives parallel genomic divergence across cities and bumble bee species
Genome Biology: Mitonuclear control of transcription complexes regulates tRNA splicing
Nucleic Acids Research: Structural basis for coupled DNA replication and uracil repair by a family of DNA polymerases from phages with T-modified genomes
item.description: Abstract Replicative DNA polymerases (DNAPs) play a critical role in genome duplication, ensuring the accurate transmission of genetic information in all domains of life. DNAPs are also essential for DNA viruses, as well as bacteriophages, where a uracil-DNA glycosylase (UDG) is often encoded in trans or is present in the DNAP gene. Here, we identify a new group of A-family DNAPs in phages that are fused to an active UDG domain and contain other large insertions. Several members of this subfamily, including phages SP-15 and YerA41, are known to be hypermodified on their thymidine base through glycosylation of a linker attached to the C5 position of thymine. We determined the atomic cryo-EM structures for two of its members in various active functional and conformational states, from YerA41 and phiLo phages. The structures reveal how these large DNAPs function as replicative DNAPs, and how they can recognize dU bases ahead of the replication fork through their UDG domain, generating abasic sites that are preferentially bypassed through dA incorporation. Such dU errors would need to be eliminated to preserve phage genome integrity. Additionally, we report the co-occurrence of both an X-family DNAP and a DNA ligase in the corresponding phage genomes and show that both enzymes can execute the final steps of base excision repair most probably on-the-fly during replication, revealing a DNA-replication-coupled repair process. The structures of these large polymerases can serve as a model of other large platform DNAPs that can recruit additional enzymatic activities necessary for phage or virus survival.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Neuronal DNA repair mediates systemic mitochondrial maintenance through acetylcholine signaling
item.description: Abstract DNA repair defects such as nucleotide excision repair (NER) mutations can lead to progeroid syndromes characterized by growth retardation and accelerated aging with distinct tissue type specific pathologies. DNA-damage-induced dysfunction of specific cell types can impair the organism’s overall function. It is unknown whether, in reverse, DNA repair in specific tissues can have non-cell-autonomous consequences on other tissues carrying DNA damage. To explore the organismal consequences of cell-type-specific DNA repair, we restricted NER activity to specific tissues and monitored consequences on organismal health in Caenorhabditis elegans . Unexpectedly, we observed that tissue-specific DNA repair is sufficient to improve overall DNA damage resistance. Strikingly, NER activity restricted to neurons only is sufficient to provide similar overall DNA damage resistance as whole-body NER in almost all tissues tested. We show that this systemic DNA damage resilience is mediated by neuronal acetylcholine signaling that promotes the maintenance of mitochondrial activity throughout the organism.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Condensins-mediated mitotic folding persists as a structural echo in interphase chromatin
item.description: Abstract The structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) protein complexes, cohesin and condensins, orchestrate cell cycle-dependent transitions in chromosome folding: from the relatively decondensed interphase chromatin, organized into dynamic DNA loops by cohesin, to the highly condensed arrays of DNA loops in mitotic chromosomes formed by condensins. Here, using Hi-C data from mouse embryonic stem cell lines with auxin-inducible degron-tagged subunits of SMC complexes, we clarify the role of condensins in shaping chromatin contacts within the interphase nucleus. We found that depletion of condensin I leads to weakened segregation of chromatin into A and B compartments. We also show that the contact patterns established by condensins during mitosis are preserved in interphase, suggesting a structural memory of mitotic chromosome folding. Condensins influence chromocenter organization: in the absence of condensin II during mitosis, centromeres tend to cluster, forming hyperclusters of pericentric heterochromatin. In contrast, depletion of condensin I reduces the number of heterochromatin clusters, consistent with enhanced chromosome territoriality. By combining a cohesin-degron system with Mcph1 knockout, we established an artificial model in which condensin II becomes the major driver of chromatin folding in interphase nuclei following cohesin depletion. Unlike extrusive cohesin, condensin II does not stall at sequence-specific sites and forms large, randomly positioned loops on interphase chromatin. Moreover, condensin II activity during interphase does not interfere with cohesin-dependent structures such as TADs and chromatin loops.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: E. coli RsmF activity depends on prior modification of 16S rRNA helix 44
item.description: Abstract Bacterial ribosomal RNA (rRNA) methylations are important for accurate translation. Four distinct methylations incorporated by RsmE, RsmF, and RsmH/ RsmI form a cluster of three modified 16S rRNA nucleotides (m 3 U1498, m 5 C1407, and m 4 Cm1402) surrounding the decoding center of the 30S subunit. Given their common substrate requirement of a late-stage intermediate 30S subunit, these enzymes likely act contemporaneously during subunit biogenesis, but whether there exists a required modification order is unknown. Here, using hypomethylated 30S subunits obtained from a collection of rsmH/I/E/F -deleted Escherichia coli strains, we identify RsmF activity to be highly dependent on prior modification of h44 both in vitro and in E. coli . RsmF activity on hypomethylated 30S subunits could be partially rescued by prior in vitro methylation using RsmE and RsmH, indicating that incorporation of these methyl groups directly shapes h44 for recognition by RsmF. RNA structure probing using selective 2′-hydroxyl acylation analyzed by primer extension and mutational profiling and molecular dynamics simulations reveal specific alterations in 16S rRNA structure and dynamics in the absence of the m 4 C1402 (RsmH) and m 3 U1498 (RsmE) modifications that likely restrict RsmF action. These studies thus uncover a previously unappreciated “order of operations” for 16S rRNA modification during ribosome biogenesis with important implications for studies on the collective functions of these modifications.

item.title: Nature Genetics: High false sign rates in transcriptome-wide association studies
item.description: This study finds that the direction of effect captured by transcriptome-wide association studies is often reversed relative to the true biological mechanism, suggesting that caution is needed when interpreting these studies and using the results for downstream applications.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Near-complete assembly of wild emmer wheat unveils centromere reorganization during polyploid evolution
item.description: A near-complete genome assembly of wild emmer wheat with resolved centromeric regions across 14 chromosomes highlights subgenome-associated patterns of centromere remodeling during wheat polyploid evolution.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Establishing Polycomb regulatory landscapes in human early development
item.description: The authors profile H2AK119ub (H2Aub) in human gametes, two-cell embryos, eight-cell embryos, blastocysts and human embryonic stem cells. Their analysis provides a comprehensive view of H2Aub reprogramming and patterning during the earliest stages of human development.

item.title: Cell Genomics: NeoBridge: Biophysics-informed neoantigen prioritization and clonal architecture profiling in pancreatic cancer
item.description: Lana Mediavilla et al. present NeoBridge, a biophysics-informed machine learning ensemble that prioritizes immunogenic neoantigens. In pancreatic cancer, subclonal neoantigen load, not clonal load, associates with worse survival, suggesting that clonal architecture should inform vaccine target selection

item.title: Cell Genomics: Detecting low-allele-fraction mosaic mutations: A multi-institution benchmarking with cell-line mixtures
item.description: Ha et al. benchmark detection strategies for mosaic mutations with low variant allele fractions (VAFs) using short- and long-read whole-genome sequencing. By cross-validating Illumina-based calls against PacBio HiFi data using cell-line mixtures generated across five institutions, they construct stratified reference sets, define realistic detection limits, and establish best practices for genome-wide analysis of low-VAF (<2%) variants in non-cancer tissues.

item.title: Cell Genomics: A pangenomic method for establishing a synthetic somatic variant resource in HapMap mixtures
item.description: Kong et al. present a comprehensive resource for benchmarking somatic variant detection across variant classes and allele fractions. Using HapMap mixtures and pangenome graphs, they establish standardized benchmarking sets for evaluating sequencing technologies and variant-calling methods.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Single-cell multiomics across nine mammals reveals cell-type-specific regulatory conservation in the brain
